blocks.text: When a function calls another function, the computer has to remember where it was — the caller's local variables and the line to come back to. It keeps that in a **stack frame**, and the frames live on the **call stack**: each call pushes a frame, each return pops one. Recursion is just a function whose frames happen to belong to itself.

blocks.alt: The call stack at the deepest moment of sumTo(3). From the bottom: main waits for sumTo(3); sumTo(3) waits to compute 3 plus something; sumTo(2) waits on 2 plus something; sumTo(1) waits on 1 plus something; and on top sumTo(0) returns 0. Five frames are alive at once. Then they pop one by one: 1, 3, 6.

blocks.text: What a call does, step by step

items: **Push**: make a new frame holding the arguments and local variables, and remember the line to return to.
**Run** the function's body. If it makes another call, that call pushes its own frame on top, and this one **pauses**.
**Pop**: on `return`, the frame is thrown away and its value is handed to the caller, which carries on from where it paused.
Only the **top** frame is ever running. Every frame below it is waiting — last in, first out, exactly like the Stack course's stack.

blocks.caption: Watch the frames pile up on the way down and pop on the way back.

blocks.text: How much memory does recursion use?

Each frame costs a little memory — tens of bytes for a small function. What matters is how many frames are alive **at the same time**, which is the **depth** of the recursion, not the total number of calls:

blocks.code:
sumTo(n)       n + 1 calls in total, n + 1 alive at once     space O(n)
fib(n)         about 2^n calls in total, only n alive at once  space O(n)
binarySearch   log n calls, log n alive at once            space O(log n)
merge sort     about 2n calls, log n deep                  space O(log n) stack + O(n) for merging

blocks.text: So when you state a recursive algorithm's space, count the **maximum depth** times the memory per frame, plus anything the function allocates. A loop doing the same job usually needs O(1).

The call stack is small — a few megabytes. Go too deep and the program crashes: **RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded** in JavaScript, **RecursionError** in Python (whose default limit is only 1,000 calls), **StackOverflowError** in Java, and a segmentation fault in C++. Roughly 10,000 frames is a safe ceiling in most languages. That's why recursion over a list of a million values is a bad idea, while recursion over a balanced tree (depth about 20) is fine.
The same sum, three ways: plain recursion, a loop, and **tail recursion**, where the recursive call is the very last thing the function does and the running total is carried along in a parameter.

A tail call leaves nothing for the caller to do, so a compiler **could** reuse the caller's frame and run it in O(1) space. Scheme and some C++ optimisers do; **JavaScript engines, Python and Java don't**. In those languages, a tail-recursive function is still O(n) deep — rewrite it as a loop when the depth can be large.

blocks.alt: Plain recursion: O(n) time, O(n) space. Loop: O(n) time, O(1) space. Tail recursion (JS / Python / Java): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Every call pushes a **frame**; every return pops one. Only the top frame runs.
Recursion's extra space is the **maximum depth** × the frame size — not the total number of calls.
Deep recursion overflows the stack: keep depth to a few thousand, or use a loop or an explicit stack.
Tail recursion only saves memory in languages that optimise it — not JavaScript, Python or Java.
